name: service-to-worker
intent: Keep request control and content retrieval ahead of presentation: a controller and dispatcher decide which command-like worker services each request, the worker populates an intermediate model from the business tier, and only then is the view selected and rendered.
problem: The presentation tier has to decide what a request means and which view shows the result, but control logic, content retrieval and view selection are scattered across the views: each page gathers its own data through the business tier, performs its own navigation and repeats the same checks, so business rules leak into markup, error and success paths diverge, and there is no single place that knows which worker handles a request or which view renders its outcome.
context: Server-side request handling where processing must precede presentation: action and form endpoints that validate input, invoke business services and then choose among success, validation-error and detail views; applications where one request may map to several views (full page, fragment, export) or several view technologies; and frameworks whose controller layer already owns routing. The pattern assumes the view is a decision of the request - a dispatcher can name the next view after the work is done - rather than something the view layer decides for itself.
benefits: Behaviour sits up front: one controller/dispatcher owns request handling, so navigation and view selection follow the same rules for every request instead of being re-decided inside each view.

Business logic moves out of templates: workers and helpers populate an intermediate model, so views shrink to rendering and the web-production and development roles stop editing the same files (the canonical 'improves role separation' consequence).
Reuse across requests, views and channels: a worker is a unit of work that several views can consume, and a view can be replaced without touching retrieval logic.

Predictable failure paths: because the worker reports the outcome and the dispatcher selects the view, validation-failure, not-found and error views are chosen by the same mechanism as the success view.
Cheaper rendering: the model is assembled once by the worker, so the template does not perform chatty service lookups while the response is being written.
Testable request logic: the worker/action can be exercised without the container or template engine, which is awkward when retrieval lives in the view.
tradeoffs: More components per request - controller, dispatcher, worker and view helper all need names, tests and wiring; for a handful of pages a Page Controller with inline retrieval is cheaper and clearer.

The intermediate model is usually an untyped contract: the worker writes keys (request attributes, ViewBag/ViewData, string-keyed template context, Rails instance variables) and the view reads them, so nothing checks that the two agree and a rename shows up as a blank field at runtime.
Fat-worker drift: the worker is a convenient place to put logic, so business rules and persistence creep out of the application/service layer into the action, duplicating or bypassing the domain.
Mixed strategies: if helpers still fetch data during rendering, content is retrieved both up front and at view time - the continuum the catalog describes - and the same work is done twice.

Centralisation cost: a single dispatcher and its mapping are a shared failure and hot configuration surface; a bad entry or a blocking call there affects every request (the canonical Consequences section itself warns about the single point of failure).
View names and mappings are commonly strings resolved at request time, so a renamed template or a mistyped action fails while serving traffic rather than at compile time.
Testing the whole path drags in the framework's dispatch machinery; workers stay unit-testable only while they are kept free of request/response types.

participants.responsibility: Initial point of contact for a request: resolves session, locale and context, performs authentication/authorization and validation, then delegates to the dispatcher and worker instead of rendering anything itself.

Owns view management and navigation: turns the logical outcome of the request into the next view (or logical view name) and vectors control to it; it may consult business state to choose, and is often encapsulated inside the controller.

Command-like component that services exactly one kind of request: invokes the business tier, updates state, populates the intermediate model the view will read, and reports the outcome the dispatcher needs to select a view.
Adapts and formats the model for display - aggregation, formatting, selecting sub-fragments - so that the view itself contains no retrieval or business logic.
Renders the model into the response (template or programmatic markup); it reads the model and owns presentation structure only.
Intermediate presentation state populated by the worker or helper and consumed by the view; ideally a typed view model rather than an attribute bag.
Business-tier entry point (application service, session facade, business delegate) through which the worker reads and writes domain state; it never knows about views.

use_cases: Server-rendered action endpoints: checkout or form submission validates input and applies a command, then renders a confirmation, an error or a redisplayed form view.
Back-office and admin applications where many pages share authentication, layout and navigation, and each page needs its own data preparation.
One request needing several views: a full page for a browser, a fragment for a partial refresh, an export or print rendering - the dispatcher decides from request state.
Multi-channel presentation where the same worker result must be rendered by different view technologies (HTML page, email body, PDF) chosen centrally instead of inside each view.
Migration of scriptlet-heavy JSP or template pages where retrieval, control and navigation must move out of the markup into workers and helpers.
HTML-over-the-wire endpoints where a worker computes a fragment model and the dispatcher selects the matching fragment template.

Rails ActionController: routing dispatches to one action method that calls the model layer and populates instance variables (the intermediate model Action View reads), and the same request's navigation is decided up front by the action's outcome - create re-renders the form with flash.now on validation failure or redirect_to on success, so view selection is a controller decision, not a template one.

Spring MVC: an @Controller method is the worker - it invokes services, fills the Model and returns a logical view name or ModelAndView, which the ViewResolver chain maps to a concrete View after the work is done; the redirect: and forward: view-name prefixes make navigation a post-processing decision with the same mechanism as the success view.

Django: a view function fetches first (get_object_or_404 raises before any rendering), places results in the context dict and returns render(request, template, context); a bound form that fails validation re-renders the form template with the bound instance - retrieval completes before template selection, and the not-found path is chosen by the same code path as the success path.
avoid_when: API-only services returning serialised data: there is no view to manage, so plain handlers returning DTOs (or an Action Domain Responder) are simpler.
Static or near-static output: a Page Controller, or a template rendered once from a file, needs none of the machinery.
A single endpoint or an early prototype: an inline handler that fetches and renders is more direct than a controller/dispatcher split.
Client-side rendering (SPA or a client framework) where the server never selects a view.
When the framework already hides the dispatcher behind a route-to-handler-to-template convention and no view-management decision remains - wiring another dispatcher on top only adds a layer.
Long-running work whose result cannot be rendered in the request context: run it asynchronously and let a later request render the outcome.
anti_patterns: Fat worker: business rules, persistence and transaction handling embedded in the action while the application/service layer is bypassed or duplicated.
Implicit model contract: workers stuffing request attributes or an untyped bag with undocumented keys that templates read, so the view's data needs are invisible and break silently.
Half-migrated views: helpers and templates still query services while the worker also retrieves data, mixing this pattern with the Dispatcher View strategy in one request.
Dispatcher god-map: a single global mapping or switch statement accumulating per-page special cases until navigation logic is configuration nobody owns.
Business logic in the template (scriptlets), which is exactly what the pattern was introduced to remove.
Dispatcher as universal decorator: the routing layer performing authentication, caching and business decisions until it becomes an untestable bottleneck.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: request control and content retrieval are separated from view selection and presentation.
Single responsibility per role: controller, dispatcher, worker, helper and view each change for one reason.
Command-style polymorphism: a new kind of request arrives as a new worker rather than as a new branch in a central conditional (open/closed principle).
Layering and dependency inversion: workers depend on business-service abstractions, views depend on a model, and neither knows the other's internals.
Information hiding: the view knows the model's contract, not how or from where the model was obtained.
best_practices: Keep workers to orchestration and model preparation; business rules belong in the service/domain layer.
Replace attribute bags with a typed view model (dedicated DTO or presentation model) so the worker-view contract is explicit and checkable.
Let the dispatcher own view selection and navigation; workers and services must contain no view names, page paths or template references.
Return the outcome explicitly (view, result object, or a logical name) so failure, validation and success paths all select a view through the same mechanism.
Keep templates logic-free and push adaptation into helpers or template functions.
Run cross-cutting work (auth, logging, tracing) in filters, middleware or interceptors around the controller rather than duplicating it per worker.
Test workers without the container and test the dispatcher mapping separately so drift in the mapping is visible.
sources: Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies (2nd ed., 2003) - Service to Worker (Presentation Tier): 'Combine a controller and dispatcher with views and helpers'; behaviour sits 'up front' in the controller and dispatcher, in contrast to the Dispatcher View strategy.
